title: "The consultant is in clinic"
topic: Working beyond competence and asking for help
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical ward. A biopsy has shown that Mr Tran, 59, has pancreatic cancer. The registrar asks you to tell him today because "the consultant is in clinic".

You have never given a diagnosis like this before and don't know what treatment options he will have.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Do it alone, as the team is busy.
options.detailed: Without the right knowledge, you may not answer his questions, which can increase his distress.

options.text: Tell the registrar you aren't ready to do this alone.
options.detailed: Breaking news of a serious cancer, without knowing the treatment options, is beyond your experience. Saying so honestly allows a better plan.

options.text: Tell Mr Tran his results aren't back yet.
options.detailed: This is a lie and would damage his trust when he finds out.

options.text: Wait until the consultant's ward round next week to tell him.
options.brief: An unnecessary delay to important news.
options.detailed: He is waiting for results. A week's delay would increase his anxiety and delay his care.

options.text: Ask if a senior can lead the conversation, with you there.
options.brief: Lets you learn, while Mr Tran gets the information he needs.
options.detailed: Joining a senior lets you see how it is done and support Mr Tran, while making sure his questions are answered.

options.text: Ask the F1 to do it, as she has done one before.
options.brief: Passes the task to someone even less experienced.
options.detailed: This doesn't solve the problem and isn't fair to the F1 or to Mr Tran.

options.text: Give Mr Tran the biopsy report to read himself.
options.detailed: Reading a cancer diagnosis without support could be very distressing and leaves his questions unanswered.

options.text: Ask the cancer nurse specialist to join you.
options.brief: Specialist support for him and for you.
options.detailed: Cancer nurse specialists are experienced in these conversations and can answer many questions and offer ongoing support.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you recognise when a task is beyond your competence and find a way to get it done well.
explanation.keyDetails: It is a serious new diagnosis. You haven't given one before. You don't know the treatment options. Support is available.
explanation.reasoning: [B] is honest about your limits, [E] keeps you involved with senior support, and [H] brings specialist help. The distractors risk a poor conversation ([A]), lie ([C]), delay ([D]), pass it on ([F]), or are impersonal ([G]).
explanation.competing: [A] may feel like being a team player, but Mr Tran deserves a conversation with someone who can answer his questions.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, working within your competence and asking for help.
